prompt: You recently completed a short exchange programme in another country. Write a text for students considering the programme in which you describe an unexpected challenge, explain what you learned from it, and give advice about how to benefit from an exchange without expecting everything to be comfortable.
requirements: Describe an unexpected challenge during the exchange.
Explain how the experience changed or taught you something.
Give practical advice to future participants.
purpose: Reflect on the experience and give useful advice
textTypeRationale: A blog combines first-person reflection with direct advice to a wider peer audience.
modelAnswerJa: 成功談だけでなく、予想外の困難から何を学んだかを中心にしています。Blogらしいpersonal voiceと読者へのadviceを組み合わせています。
modelAnswer:
The Best Part of My Exchange Was the Week I Wanted to Go Home

Before my exchange programme, I imagined the difficult parts would be obvious: speaking another language, finding my way around a new city and missing my family. I prepared for all of those. What I did not prepare for was feeling lonely even when I was surrounded by people.

My host family was kind, and my classmates included me in activities, but during the second week I became exhausted. Every conversation required concentration. Jokes moved too quickly, school routines were unfamiliar, and by the evening I wanted silence more than adventure. I started comparing the real experience with the exciting version I had imagined before leaving home. The real one seemed to be failing.

The turning point came when I admitted this to my host sister. I expected her to think I was ungrateful. Instead, she laughed and told me she had felt exactly the same during her exchange the previous year. She explained that being uncomfortable did not mean the programme was going badly; it meant I was living without my normal routines and support systems.

After that conversation, I changed my approach. I stopped trying to make every day impressive. I allowed myself quiet evenings, asked more questions when I did not understand something, and kept a small notebook of phrases I wanted to use again. I also started saying yes to ordinary activities such as grocery shopping and helping cook dinner. Those moments taught me more about daily life than several organized sightseeing trips.

The experience changed how I think about confidence. I used to imagine confidence as feeling certain and relaxed. During the exchange, confidence often meant doing something while feeling awkward. Ordering food after making a mistake the day before, joining a conversation when I knew I would miss half the jokes, or asking someone to repeat a sentence required more courage than any tourist activity.

If you are considering an exchange, my first piece of advice is to expect a difficult period. Do not treat homesickness or tiredness as evidence that you made the wrong decision. Second, build small routines. A regular walk, a weekly call home or time to write can give you stability. Third, be curious about ordinary life. Ask why people do things differently instead of deciding immediately that your way is better.

Finally, remember that an exchange is not a performance. You do not need to return with perfect language skills, hundreds of photographs or a completely new personality. The goal is to pay attention, adapt and notice what you take for granted at home.

My best memories now include the uncomfortable week because it forced me to stop being a visitor and start learning how to live somewhere unfamiliar. That was the moment the exchange became real.

prompt: Your school is planning an overseas trip and wants students to think about responsible tourism. Write a text for a school meeting in which you explain how tourism can benefit and harm local communities, recommend responsible behaviour, and persuade students that a successful trip is more than seeing famous places.
requirements: Explain both benefits and possible harms of tourism.
Persuade students to value learning and respect over simply collecting experiences.
audience: Students and teachers preparing for an overseas trip
purpose: Promote responsible tourism before the trip
textTypeRationale: A speech is appropriate for a school meeting because it can address the group directly, acknowledge excitement and set shared expectations.
modelAnswerJa: 旅行への期待を壊さず、local communityへの影響を考えさせる構成です。Speechとしてaudienceを直接巻き込み、具体的な行動に結びつけています。
modelAnswer:
Good afternoon everyone,

In a few months, many of us will be travelling overseas together. We are already talking about the places we want to see, the food we want to try and the photographs we hope to take. Excitement is part of travel, but before we leave, we should also ask a less comfortable question: what kind of visitors do we want to be?

Tourism can bring real benefits. Visitors spend money in restaurants, hotels, museums and local shops. They can support jobs and help fund the protection of cultural sites. Meeting people from different places can also reduce stereotypes, especially when travellers are willing to listen rather than only observe.

However, tourism can create problems too. Popular areas may become crowded, housing can become more expensive when apartments are converted into short-term rentals, and local traditions may be treated as entertainment instead of living culture. Environmental pressure increases when large numbers of visitors use water, transport and fragile natural spaces.

Our school trip will not solve these global problems, but our behaviour still matters. First, we should spend responsibly. When possible, we can use locally owned businesses rather than buying everything from international chains. That does not mean assuming that every small business is automatically ethical. It simply means noticing where our money goes and making informed choices.

Second, we should treat photography as a privilege, not a right. A beautiful market, religious ceremony or neighbourhood is not a film set created for us. If people are clearly identifiable, we should ask before taking close photographs. If a site has rules about clothing, noise or restricted areas, we should follow them even when nobody appears to be watching.

Third, we should reduce waste and unnecessary consumption. Carrying a refillable bottle where safe, avoiding single-use items and using public transport when practical are small actions, but they help us travel with less impact.

Most importantly, we should leave time for learning. A successful trip is not measured by how many famous locations we can photograph in one day. It is measured by whether we understand something we did not understand before. Talking with local guides, learning a few useful phrases and asking thoughtful questions can make a place more than a background for our social media accounts.

Some people may say this approach makes travel too serious. I disagree. Respect does not remove fun. In fact, paying attention usually makes travel more interesting because we notice details that hurried tourists miss.

We are guests in someone else’s everyday environment. If we remember that simple fact, we can enjoy the trip while also respecting the people who will still be there after our buses leave.

Let us return home with photographs, certainly, but also with better questions, deeper understanding and the knowledge that we travelled responsibly.

Thank you.

prompt: A close friend is discouraged after failing to reach an important personal goal. Write a text in which you describe a similar experience of your own, explain what helped you respond constructively, and give advice without pretending that failure is always positive.
requirements: Describe a relevant personal experience of failure or disappointment.
Explain what helped you respond constructively.
Give realistic advice without romanticizing failure.
purpose: Offer honest support based on personal experience
textTypeRationale: A personal letter fits the close relationship and allows empathy, self-disclosure and direct advice.
modelAnswerJa: 『失敗は必ず良い経験になる』と単純化せず、友人への共感と具体的な助言を中心にしています。Personal letterとして距離感の近いtoneを維持しています。
modelAnswer:
Dear Leo,

I heard about the competition result, and I know how much work you put into it. I am not going to tell you that everything happens for a reason or that failing is secretly wonderful. Sometimes disappointment is simply painful, especially when the goal mattered.

Last year I had a similar experience with the school debate team. I had spent months preparing for selection and was convinced I had improved enough to make the final group. When the results were posted, my name was not there. What made it worse was seeing two close friends selected. I was happy for them and jealous at the same time, which made me feel guilty as well as disappointed.

For the first few days, I tried to turn the result into a dramatic lesson immediately. I told myself I would work twice as hard and prove everyone wrong. That motivation lasted about forty-eight hours. What actually helped was much less dramatic.

First, I allowed myself to be disappointed without turning the result into a judgment about my entire ability. I had failed one selection process. That was different from being a failure. It sounds like a small difference in language, but it changed how I thought about the situation.

Second, I asked the coach for specific feedback. I expected a general answer, but she explained that my ideas were strong while my delivery became rushed under pressure. That gave me something practical to work on. I started recording short speeches, watching them back and deliberately slowing down. I hated doing this at first, but it was more useful than simply telling myself to improve.

Third, I stayed involved. I helped the selected team research arguments and attended practice sessions. This was difficult because it reminded me that I had not been chosen, but it also stopped me from turning disappointment into isolation. I learned from people who were better than me in certain areas, and I realized that the selection result had not removed my connection to debating.

I do not know yet what your result will mean for your goal. Maybe it will push you in a new direction. Maybe you will try again and succeed. Maybe you will eventually decide the goal is no longer worth the cost. All of those possibilities are valid.

My advice is not to force a positive meaning too quickly. Give yourself time, then separate what you can control from what you cannot. Ask for useful feedback, choose one or two changes, and decide later whether you still want the same goal.

You are allowed to be disappointed because you cared. Just do not let one result make every decision for you.

Call me when you feel like talking — or when you want to avoid talking and just get food.

Take care,

Sam
